That is,

  • the element in the [MATH: i]th row and [MATH: j]th column for [MATH: i \neq j] is [MATH: \Sigma_{ij} = \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j].]

Now, note that [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{Cov}[Y,X].] As a result, the covariance matrix is always symmetric (moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix).

So, we can find the missing elements as follows:

  • [MATH: a = \Sigma_{21} = \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_1] = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2] = \Sigma_{12} = 2]

  • [MATH: b = \Sigma_{23} = \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = \textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_2] = \Sigma_{32} = 1]

  • [MATH: c = \Sigma_{31} = \textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_1] = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_3] = \Sigma_{13} = 0]

Therefore, [MATH: a + b + c = 2 + 1 +0 = 3.]

sections.normalized_html:
For two random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] the covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma] is given by

[MATH: [Var[X]|Cov[X, Y]; Cov[Y, X]|Var[Y]]]

Recall that the variance of a random variable [MATH: X] is determined by the formula

[MATH: \textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \textrm{E}[X]^2,]

and the covariance of two random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is given by the formula

[MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X] \cdot \textrm{E}[Y].]

First, let's find [MATH: \textrm{Var}[X]{:}]

[MATH: Var[X]|= E[X^{2}] − E[X]^{2}; = 18 − 4^{2}; = 2]

Similarly,

[MATH: Var[Y]|= E[Y^{2}] − E[Y]^{2}; = 14 − 3^{2}; = 5.]

Now lets find [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y]{:}]

[MATH: Cov[X, Y]|= E[XY] − E[X] ⋅ E[Y]; = 9 − 4 ⋅ 3; = − 3]

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

[MATH: [Var[X]|Cov[X, Y]; Cov[Y, X]|Var[Y]]]

Note the following:

Content:
- The [MATH: i]th diagonal element is [MATH: \Sigma_{ii} = \textrm{Var}[X_i].]
- The element in the [MATH: i]th row and [MATH: j]th column for [MATH: i \neq j] is [MATH: \Sigma_{ij} = \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j].]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X_i,X_j] = \textrm{Cov}[X_j,X_i]] for any pair of random variables [MATH: X_i, X_j], we have the following theorem:

Content:
> The covariance matrix is always symmetric. Moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix.

Item 2 — Example: Determining Elements of a Covariance Matrix

For random variables [MATH: X_1, \ldots, X_n,] the covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma] is given by

That is,

- the [MATH: i]th diagonal element is [MATH: \Sigma_{ii} = \textrm{Var}[X_i],] and
- the element in the [MATH: i]th row and [MATH: j]th column for [MATH: i \neq j] is [MATH: \Sigma_{ij} = \textrm{Cov}[X_i, X_j].]

Now, note that
[MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{Cov}[Y,X].]
As a result, the covariance matrix is always symmetric (moreover, it is a positive semi-definite matrix).

So, we can find the missing elements as follows:

- [MATH: b = \Sigma_{23} = \textrm{Cov}[X_2,X_3] = \textrm{Cov}[X_3,X_2] = \Sigma_{32} = 1]
